items.title: Thalamic oscillations distinguish natural states of consciousness in humans
items.summary: Direct recordings in a human clinical sample identified a roughly 19–45 Hz central-thalamic rhythm during wakefulness and REM sleep, absent during non-REM sleep in these recordings. The result offers a target for studying how deep brain systems regulate states. It is an association in the studied conditions, not a universal test for conscious experience; non-REM sleep can also include experience.
items.headline: Thalamic recordings reveal a rhythm associated with wakefulness and REM sleep

explainer.finding: A rhythm in a deep brain structure differed between recorded waking, REM, and non-REM states in a human clinical sample.
explainer.method: Researchers compared direct central-thalamic recordings across those states and identified activity around 19–45 Hz during wakefulness and REM in their data.
explainer.meaning: A state-linked rhythm can give researchers a target for testing how brain systems regulate waking and sleep—much as a useful indicator helps locate a process to investigate.
explainer.limits: Tracking these states does not establish a universal consciousness test. The sample and recording conditions matter, and experience can occur during non-REM sleep.

items.title: The act of detecting a stimulus contaminates measures of conscious experience with decision biases
items.authors: Nicolás Sánchez-Fuenzalida, Chris Jungerius, Stephen M. Fleming
items.summary: Experiments with 505 participants combined detection judgments and reproductions of faint visual stimuli. Changes in base rates and rewards affected response criteria, while attention affected a modeled perceptual component. Adding detection judgments also influenced reproduction reports. The study shows why reporting a signal and experiencing it need careful separation; its decomposition depends on the model and tasks used.
items.headline: Saying whether a faint image appeared can change how perception is measured

explainer.finding: A person’s decision to report a faint image can affect measurements intended to describe their visual experience.
explainer.method: Experiments with 505 participants combined detection judgments and stimulus reproductions, varying factors such as rewards, base rates, and attention.
explainer.meaning: Saying “yes, I saw it” can reflect both sensory information and how willing someone is to risk a false alarm. Separating those helps prevent a decision change from being called a perceptual change.
explainer.limits: The separation relies on the tasks and model used. The study does not supply an assumption-free way to measure subjective experience.

items.title: Adversarial testing of global neuronal workspace and integrated information theories of consciousness
items.summary: The consortium preregistered competing predictions and measured brain activity while 256 people viewed clearly visible stimuli. Results matched some predictions and challenged key commitments of both integrated information and global neuronal workspace theories. The work tests specified claims about visual experience; it neither settles consciousness nor establishes a different theory by elimination.
items.headline: A joint experiment challenges predictions from two consciousness theories

explainer.finding: A shared experiment supported some predictions and challenged important commitments of two consciousness theories.
explainer.method: Advocates agreed on divergent predictions in advance, and the consortium recorded brain activity while 256 people viewed clearly visible stimuli.
explainer.meaning: Agreeing on the test beforehand makes it harder for each group to select only favorable results afterward. The mismatches identify where theories need clearer explanations and fresh predictions.
explainer.limits: These are tests of specified claims about visual experience. They do not settle consciousness as a whole or prove another theory true by elimination.

items.title: Functional connectomics spanning multiple areas of mouse visual cortex
items.summary: The project paired calcium imaging of about 75,000 neurons with electron-microscopy reconstructions containing more than 200,000 cells and roughly half a billion synapses. Researchers can investigate how measured responses relate to physical connections in visual cortex. This is an open resource from one mouse, with reconstruction and sampling limits; a wiring diagram does not by itself explain a mind.
items.headline: A mouse-brain dataset links neural activity with detailed wiring

explainer.finding: An open mouse-brain dataset connects recorded neural responses with an unusually detailed reconstruction of physical wiring.
explainer.method: The project paired calcium imaging of about 75,000 neurons with electron-microscopy reconstructions containing more than 200,000 cells and roughly half a billion synapses.
explainer.meaning: A road map and a record of traffic answer different questions. Having both helps researchers investigate how connections relate to activity.
explainer.limits: The resource comes from one mouse and contains sampling and reconstruction limits. Wiring plus recorded activity does not by itself explain every computation or experience.

items.title: A streaming brain-to-voice neuroprosthesis to restore naturalistic communication
items.summary: In one clinical-trial participant with severe paralysis, a system used cortical surface recordings and trained neural networks to synthesize speech in a continuous stream. Decoding proceeded in 80-millisecond increments. The demonstration targets attempted speech under a specialized recording and training setup; it does not establish general thought reading or equivalent performance across people.
items.headline: A trained brain interface turns attempted speech into streaming audio

explainer.finding: A trained brain interface converted one participant’s attempted speech into continuously generated audio.
explainer.method: The system used cortical surface recordings and trained neural networks, decoding in 80-millisecond increments in a clinical-trial participant with severe paralysis.
explainer.meaning: Streaming can reduce the need to wait for an entire attempted utterance before hearing output, an important feature for conversational turn-taking.
explainer.limits: This specialized, trained setup targets attempted speech. It does not establish unrestricted thought reading or the same performance in other people.

items.title: Sleep microstructure organizes memory replay
items.authors: Hongyu Chang, Wenbo Tang et al.
items.summary: Simultaneous neural recordings and pupil measurements distinguished non-REM sleep substates associated with replay of recent versus older experiences. Disrupting sharp-wave ripples in the recent-memory-associated substate impaired later recall. The experiment links timing to a memory effect in mice; it is not evidence that monitoring or changing human pupil size can improve learning.
items.headline: Mouse sleep substates separate replay of recent and older memories

explainer.finding: Different substates of mouse non-REM sleep were associated with replay of recent and older experiences.
explainer.method: Researchers recorded neural activity and pupils, then disrupted sharp-wave ripples in the substate linked to recent memories; later recall was impaired.
explainer.meaning: The intervention connects the timing of neural events with a memory outcome. It helps explain why treating all of sleep as one uniform state can miss useful structure.
explainer.limits: This is evidence from mice under specific conditions. It does not show that changing human pupil size or using a consumer sleep tracker improves learning.

items.title: Quantifying the prevalence and impact of overreaching causal claims in social science
items.headline: Causal wording changes how readers interpret correlational studies
items.authors: Calvin Isch, Timothy Dörr, Neil Fasching, Grace Jennings, Duncan J. Watts
items.summary: A corpus analysis found frequent causal wording in cross-sectional research. Separate reader experiments showed that phrasing affects interpretation. Classification and sampling constrain the prevalence estimate.

evidence.question: Does wording overstate causal evidence?
evidence.method: Validated text classification and reader experiments.
evidence.limitations: The selected corpus does not represent every study design.

explainer.finding: Causal language can strengthen readers’ causal interpretations.
explainer.method: Readers encountered original or associationally rewritten abstracts.
explainer.limits: Corpus prevalence depends on classification; experimental results concern the tested reading tasks.

editorialReview.reason: Primary study followed from a research briefing; separates corpus analysis from reader experiments.

items.title: Reciprocal connections dynamically build consensus between neocortical areas
items.headline: How two mouse visual areas settle into agreement
items.authors: Mitra Javadzadeh, Marine Schimel, Sonja B. Hofer, Yashar Ahmadian and Guillaume Hennequin
items.summary: Reanalyzed mouse recordings support models in which communication between visual areas sustains matching activity patterns. A simple visual task cannot establish a general explanation of consciousness.

evidence.question: How do visual areas coordinate their activity?
evidence.method: Existing recordings and light-based neural suppression; circuit models fitted to seven mice, timing analyses using twelve.
evidence.limitations: Two mouse areas; sensory, movement, and reward signals overlap.

explainer.finding: Matching activity patterns persisted longer than conflicting ones, as the circuit models predicted.
explainer.method: Researchers reanalyzed simultaneous V1 and LM recordings during a rewarded tilted-stripe task, including brief suppression of either area.
explainer.meaning: Think of recognizing a stripe's tilt: feedback could help separate areas maintain a consistent interpretation.
explainer.limits: This mechanism remains model-dependent. Broader brain functions and human subjective experience were not tested.

editorialReview.reason: Read results, experimental procedures, and discussion; teaches network coordination.

items.title: Comprehensive profiling of brain dynamics during anesthesia across phylogeny
items.headline: Under anesthesia, brain signals lose persistence and coordination
items.summary: Across six species, measured neural signals became less persistent and synchronized under anesthesia. This shared pattern is not a universal test of consciousness.

evidence.question: Do different anesthetics produce shared changes in neural activity?
evidence.method: Compared 6,827 signal features using mammalian fMRI and zebrafish/nematode calcium imaging; the human sample included 15 healthy men.
evidence.limitations: Small samples, different drugs, doses, and recording methods limit comparisons.

explainer.finding: Slow signals retained less similarity to their recent past, and activity across regions became less coordinated.
explainer.method: Researchers compared awake and anesthetized recordings, with permutation checks for chance consistency.
explainer.meaning: In two macaques, targeted thalamic stimulation restored behavioral responsiveness and shifted signals toward the awake pattern despite continued anesthesia.
explainer.limits: Responsiveness does not directly measure subjective experience. These slow imaging signals also differ from fast electrical brain rhythms.

editorialReview.reason: Read primary results, methods, statistics, and limitations; separates neural measurements from subjective experience.

items.title: A half-center oscillator regulates sleep pressure
items.authors: Peter S. Hasenhuetl, Raffaele Sarnataro, Eleftheria Vrontou, H. Olof Rorsman, Clifford B. Talbot, Ruth Brain, Gero Miesenböck
items.headline: A fly brain circuit keeps a running signal of sleep need
items.summary: Neural rhythms can do more than accompany sleep. In fruit flies, researchers found that two interacting groups of sleep-control neurons generate slow oscillations whose strength rises after sleep loss. Disrupting their chemical communication reduced normal and recovery sleep; replaying burst-like activity with light increased sleep. The rhythm also persisted during wakefulness, suggesting a signal of sleep need rather than a simple asleep-or-awake indicator. This is evidence from flies, not a demonstrated human sleep mechanism.

evidence.question: How do sleep-control neurons represent sleep need, and does their rhythmic activity help cause sleep?
evidence.method: In young adult female Drosophila, combined calcium imaging, electrical recordings, connectome analysis, targeted genetic interference and optogenetic stimulation. Compared rested and sleep-deprived flies and rhythmic versus evenly spaced stimulation. Behavioral sleep was scored from approximately five minutes of inactivity, with arousal and locomotion checks.
evidence.limitations: Imaging captures only some activity patterns, and sleep is behaviorally defined rather than measured with human sleep-stage criteria. Genetic targeting and stimulation are experimental manipulations; the downstream conversion of continuous sleep pressure into sleep remains unresolved.

explainer.finding: The two neuronal groups inhibit one another across the brain’s midline and alternate activity. Oscillation strength increased after sleep deprivation and declined during recovery. Interfering with glutamate release weakened both the rhythm and sleep.
explainer.method: Light-sensitive proteins let researchers stimulate selected neurons. Bursts resembling the natural rhythm promoted sleep more effectively than spreading the same pulse count evenly through time; genetic interference supplied a complementary test of the circuit’s contribution.
explainer.meaning: Think of a tiredness gauge that keeps running even while an animal is awake. A separate decision is still needed to turn that changing signal into sleep. The experiments help separate those two functions.
explainer.limits: The study does not show that humans use the same circuit or that changing brain rhythms would treat insomnia. The authors propose several ways downstream neurons might select sleep, but do not establish which one operates.

editorialReview.reason: Read primary results, interference and replay experiments, behavioral and imaging methods, and discussion. Explains causal circuit testing while preserving the fruit-fly model, behavioral sleep definition and unresolved downstream mechanism.

items.title: Long-term development of a motor memory
items.headline: Extended practice makes a motor memory more durable—and more specific
items.authors: David W. Franklin, Pascal Nietschmann and Sae Franklin
items.summary: Getting a movement right today and retaining it months later are different achievements. In two experiments with 28 young adults, participants repeatedly reached while a robot pushed their hand sideways. Across eight training sessions, they learned to anticipate nearly all of that push. At a return visit 15 weeks later, they retained about 60% of the learned compensating force before retraining. Practice also narrowed how broadly the response carried over to other reaching directions. The result shows continuing refinement after initial success, but it comes from one laboratory movement task, not a test of sports training or rehabilitation.

evidence.question: How does extended training change the strength, retention and generalization of adaptation to a predictable sideways force?
evidence.method: Ten participants trained in eight weekly sessions; a second, preregistered experiment with 18 participants used eight sessions within four weeks. Both groups returned 15 weeks after training. Participants reached with their dominant right hand against a velocity-dependent robotic force. Occasional trials constrained the hand to a straight channel, measuring anticipatory force independently of sideways movement errors. Other probes tested nearby directions and the untrained hand.
evidence.limitations: The samples were small, young, healthy and right-handed. The task trained a single reaching direction, and no clinical or real-world skill outcome was measured. These behavioral measures cannot identify the neural mechanism or establish an optimal practice schedule. The roughly 60% retention concerns compensating force relative to the previous session, not a percentage of all skill or memory.

explainer.finding: Compensation improved across training, while retention became stronger and generalization to other directions narrowed. At the 15-week return, about 60% of the learned force pattern remained. Transfer to the untrained left hand stayed limited.
explainer.method: The robot sometimes acted like a narrow rail. By measuring the force participants applied against it, the researchers could tell whether they anticipated the usual sideways push. Testing this way at the start of the return visit helped separate retained learning from rapid relearning.
explainer.meaning: Imagine learning to reach straight ahead despite a steady sideways disturbance. You can become better at that precise movement without gaining equally across every other direction. The study illustrates why accuracy, lasting retention and transfer should be measured separately when evaluating practice.
explainer.limits: This was a robotic reaching task in 28 adults. It does not show how many repetitions a musician, athlete or patient needs, and it did not measure brain activity or compare rehabilitation treatments.

editorialReview.reason: Read primary participant and task methods, force-channel analysis, adaptation, generalization, retention, transfer and discussion. Teaches the distinction between initial performance, durable retention and transfer. Preserves small healthy samples, task specificity and behavioral rather than neural evidence; does not turn the authors' rehabilitation implications into a tested treatment.

items.title: Causal role of human hippocampus in relational structure learning and inference
items.headline: The hippocampus helps people use a pattern to infer a missing relationship
items.authors: Deng Pan, Simone D’Ambrogio, Naomi Kingston, Miruna Rascu, Pranav Sankhe, Shuyi Luo, Miriam C. Klein-Flügge, Ali Mahmoodi and Matthew F. S. Rushworth
items.summary: If four characters always form two pairs, discovering one pair tells you something about the other. In a football-themed prediction game, participants used this kind of structure to adapt when pairings changed. Brain scans in 36 people linked that structure to hippocampal activity. In a separate group of 20, ultrasound targeting the hippocampus reduced a behavioural measure of structure-based inference compared with stimulation at a control site. Overall prediction accuracy did not show a detectable change. The result supports a role for the hippocampus and its connected network in this specific kind of learning, rather than showing that stimulation erased memories or reasoning generally.

evidence.question: Does the human hippocampus help learners infer changing relationships from an abstract structure learned previously?
evidence.method: Participants learned probabilistic transitions among four characters arranged in two pairs, then predicted shots in a game with changing pairings and shot preferences. The study combined fMRI in 36 participants, computational models and a separate counterbalanced within-person ultrasound experiment in 20 participants. Each person received hippocampal and white-matter control-site stimulation in sessions at least one week apart. Two additional groups of 40 completed behavioural experiments without stimulation, including one with revised instructions.
evidence.limitations: The ultrasound sample consisted of selected healthy adults aged 19–33; 32 were initially scanned, 23 met simulation-based targeting criteria and 20 completed both sessions. Participants were blinded, but the experimenter was not, and none of the experiments was preregistered. Inference was estimated from choices in a constrained task. Stimulation can affect connected regions, and no detectable overall-accuracy effect is not proof of no such effect.

explainer.finding: Hippocampal stimulation reduced how strongly both direct pair experience and information about the other pair guided behaviour, especially early in learning. The inference effect was reduced relative to control stimulation (Cohen’s d = −0.89; 95% confidence interval −1.41 to −0.36). Learning individual characters’ shot preferences and overall prediction accuracy showed no statistically detectable changes.
explainer.method: The key comparison separated seeing a pair directly from inferring it after seeing the other pair. Brain imaging tested whether activity patterns reflected that structure. A recurrent neural network generated predictions about disrupting structure representations; the separate ultrasound experiment then tested whether targeting the hippocampus changed human behaviour relative to an active control site.
explainer.meaning: Knowing that A pairs with B lets you infer that C pairs with D when the rule is two pairs among four characters. You do not need to observe every connection from scratch. The experiment tests how a learned pattern can help fill in missing information when the particular characters or pairings change.
explainer.limits: A network simulation is not a biological account of how hippocampal neurons work. The stimulation result supports causal involvement of the hippocampus and possibly its broader network, not an isolated brain region responsible for all inference. Small selected samples and this artificial task limit generalization to everyday learning; this was not a treatment or memory-improvement trial.

editorialReview.reason: Read primary task design, behavioural and fMRI results, network-lesion predictions, ultrasound intervention, discussion, participant selection, blinding, stimulation and statistical methods. Explains inference from a learned relational structure while distinguishing neural correlations, model predictions and intervention evidence. Preserves the null overall-accuracy result, small selected sample, lack of preregistration and possible connected-network effects.
